input:
An inventory policy has been specified for a spare motor using a statistical model of weekly demand. Mean demand is 2183 units per week, with a standard deviation of 592 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 9 weeks. On this basis, the safety stock required for a 95% cycle service level is 2930 units. The calculation is based on the assumption that demand can be treated as normal and that demand in individual weeks is independent. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy basis. Consequently, the safety-stock figure is intended to address variability represented by the stated demand distribution during the replenishment period, but it should not be interpreted as providing the same service protection during seasonal demand peaks that fall outside the assumptions used to establish it.

In practical terms, the safety stock is not intended to satisfy average demand; average demand during the lead time is the background against which the buffer is held. The buffer addresses the possibility that demand in particular weeks will be above the mean while replenishment is still in transit. The normal-demand assumption gives that variability a particular shape, and the independence assumption means that a high-demand week is not treated as making another high-demand week more likely. If either assumption fails, the same numerical buffer may not deliver the intended service level. The exclusion of seasonal peaks is therefore not a minor qualification. A peak is a patterned increase in demand rather than random week-to-week variation, and a policy built only on the stated distribution does not claim to absorb it.
target:
Inventory policy for a spare motor sets safety stock at 2930 units for a 95% cycle service level. Mean demand is 2183 units per week, the standard deviation is 592 units per week, and replenishment lead time is 9 weeks.

Safety stock is the buffer held against demand variability over the exposure created by lead time. The service level states the cycle-service criterion used to set the buffer; it is not a guarantee that every replenishment cycle will be covered. The stated mean fixes the expected demand rate, the standard deviation fixes the variability admitted by the model, and lead time fixes the period over which that variability matters. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks. Seasonal peaks are excluded. The policy therefore covers the modelled week-to-week variation on the stated basis, but it does not size the buffer for a seasonal peak, a change in mean demand, or dependence between weekly demands.

Safety stock is not stock for mean demand. Mean demand is met by the normal replenishment flow; the buffer covers demand above the mean during the lead-time exposure. The normal assumption gives the admitted variability a symmetric distribution around the mean, and independence means a high-demand week does not change the expectation for the next week. Both assumptions are part of the result. If weekly demands are correlated, or if the mean shifts, the same buffer no longer carries the same service meaning. Seasonal peaks are excluded for that reason: a patterned rise in demand is not the random variation the buffer was sized to absorb. The figure should be reviewed when the demand pattern, lead time, or service criterion changes, because each belongs to the basis on which the buffer was set.
